articles.title: Rajasthan Govt Partners With M1xchange, RXIL To Boost TReDS Adoption Among MSMEs
articles.description: Rajasthan Govt Partners With M1xchange, RXIL To Boost TReDS Adoption Among MSMEs Jaipur, Oct 8 (KNN) Rajasthan’s Department of Industries and Commerce has signed agreements with M1xchange and Receivables Exchange of India Ltd (RXIL) to expand adoption of the Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS) among micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), aiming to address delayed payments and improve access to working capital. TReDS enables MSMEs to convert accepted invoices into early payments by allowing authorised financiers to discount receivables at competitive rates. This can reduce dependence on costly short-term borrowing and help smaller firms manage wages, raw material purchases and production. The initiative comes amid stronger regulatory focus on payment discipline. A November 7, 2024 notification made TReDS registration mandatory for companies with turnover above ₹250 crore and all central public sector enterprises. A June 30 notification further required operating central public sector enterprises to settle MSME purchase invoices through RBI-authorised platforms, The Economic Times reported. To support implementation, the Department has circulated a standard operating procedure (SOP) to state departments and related bodies, covering departments, boards, corporations, authorities, institutions and MSME vendors and suppliers. Under the agreements, the department will work with M1xchange and RXIL to promote TReDS adoption, create awareness and support relevant stakeholders in using the platform. The move is aimed at making faster invoice realisation part of procurement efficiency while improving liquidity for MSMEs. Faster payments can help smaller firms avoid production disruptions, manage demand fluctuations and take on additional orders without relying heavily on debt. Rajasthan’s initiative also aligns with the broader national push to bring more large buyers and public sector entities onto TReDS, potentially making digital invoice financing a more routine source of working capital for MSMEs. (KNN Bureau)

articles.title: Narendra Modi: The living sage-statesman among the venerable stalwarts of the past
articles.description: On the occasion of Prime Minister Narendra Modi completing 25 years as Head of Government and marking his 76th birthday, it is an appropriate moment to reflect on the remarkable journey of a public life shaped by spiritual discipline, national service, cultural rootedness and an unwavering commitment to the idea of Bharat. On October 7, 2026, Narendra Modi completed 25 continuous years at the helm of government, beginning with his assumption of office as Chief Minister of Gujarat in 2001 and continuing as Prime Minister of India since 2014. His 76th birthday, celebrated on September 17, 2026, provided another occasion to recall the values and influences that have shaped his public life. After undergoing rigorous spiritual discipleship at the Vivekananda Math, Narendra Damodardas Modi was initiated into spiritual wisdom. During his residence at Belur Math and the Rajkot Ramakrishna Ashram, the youthful Narendra Modi immersed himself heart and soul in the teachings of the warrior-monk, Swami Vivekananda. From Vivekananda, he indelibly inscribed upon his tender mind ideals of a culturally rooted spiritual society, economic equity, political liberty, pristine moral virtue, intellectual growth, sublime cultural heritage, and reciprocal human respect. Young Narendra Modi received stirring counsels of Swami Vivekananda as sacred Deeksha from Swami Atmasthanandaji Maharaj, the revered leader and spiritual beacon of the Ramakrishna Order. Holding also Swami Dayananda Saraswati as his spiritual guru, Prime Minister Narendra Modi maintains a profound personal bond with the Ramakrishna Math, forged under the tutelage of Swami Atmasthanandaji. Also Read: 25 years of leadership: PM Modi sets ‘We will do it’ mantra, puts India’s 2047 ambitions on a war footing In a public life spanning sixty-five years, including over twenty-six years presiding at the pinnacles of state and national governance as Chief Minister of a powerhouse state and Prime Minister of India, not a single blemish of corruption has ever been substantiated against Narendra Modi. How has he stood as the devoted son of this sacred land—an upright, uncorrupted, transparent, and truthful statesman? In the hearts of 1.48 billion people of multifaceted languages, races, arts, and cultures, he dwells with unassuming simplicity: as a man of impeccable integrity, an illustrious son of the soil, and a resolute guardian of the masses. Guided by the sublime vision of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam—the world is one family—he has striven tirelessly to champion a borderless humanism transcending caste, creed, and nationality, fostering global harmony and mutual cooperation. No discerning citizen can dispute that Prime Minister Modi acts with utmost vigilance in nurturing India’s international relations: undertaking official visits to over a hundred nations, receiving the highest civilian honours from thirty-four sovereign states, and addressing the parliaments of seventy nations, shining across global forums with intellectual majesty. While a few myopic detractors within India have sought to confine him to partisan labels, the citizenry has thoroughly unmasked their rhetoric; notably, it is Islamic nations that have conferred upon him several of their highest civilian accolades. I venture here to present a panoramic comparison between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the towering political luminaries of India, particularly the beloved icons of Tamil Nadu. Like a feline aspiring to lap up the vast ocean, my deep devotion to Modi’s ideals will carry it through. Narendra Modi is giving living reality on the Indian political landscape to the sublime dreams of those selfless souls of freedom fighters who offered their blood, toil, sweat, and very lives. The resolute vow to protect this motherland and breathe life into the vision sketched by our forebears was carved into his consciousness as an eighteen-year-old youth. Long before assuming office as the Chief Minister of Gujarat on October 7, 2001, he traversed the length and breadth of India, mingling intimately with common citizens and discerning firsthand the trials of their existence. Like a penetrating beam, he absorbed the philosophies, selfless service, industry, sacrifice, and patriotism of our ancestors, evolving into a vessel of mature wisdom. Also Read: International Awards Conferred to Narendra Modi: A testament to expanding global influence of India Ever since receiving initiation, Narendra Modi has marched forward with an identical indomitable spirit, impassioned by the unity, prosperity, and global stature of India. Struck with awe at Netaji’s valour, Modi imbibed that very intrepidity into his life. Narendra Modi measures his days entirely through dedicated public service. Pondering the welfare of the citizenry round the clock through sweat, sacrifice, and total devotion, he has occupied the highest corridors of power for twenty-six years without allowing the faintest trace of hubris or arrogance to touch him. Adhering to an ascetic personal discipline, his governance philosophy—Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas—embodies equitable development embracing every citizen without distinction of caste or creed. It represents a collective endeavour where welfare schemes and fundamental amenities reach the poorest uninterrupted. Uprooting terrorism through decisive cross-border security operations reflects the martial resolve of Subhas Chandra Bose; similarly, the Gandhian paradigm of indigenous economic production is reborn in Modi’s Make in India and Made in India economic renaissance. In 1857, Veer Vinayak Damodar Savarkar sounded a clarion call to Hindus and Muslims alike: “Where is our wealth? Where is our land? Where is our strength? All lie eclipsed beneath the yoke of bondage! If we forfeit the fortitude to shield our faith and motherland, the sin of their destruction shall rest squarely upon our own shoulders.” Savarkar’s rallying cry ignited a volcanic eruption among the populace, sparking the First War of Independence. Today, Modi has resolved historical fissures born of that struggle; the triumphant fluttering of the tricolour across the hamlets of Kashmir and the reverberating echoes of Bharat Mata Ki Jai stand as testament. Drawing comparisons between Prime Minister Modi and the legendary stalwarts of Tamil Nadu’s political history serves to illustrate the profound kinship of spirit that exists between the Prime Minister and the ethos of Tamil self-sacrifice. articles.title: Two Hills Cut, Khamrenga Beel Almost Filled: What is Happening Near Amchang Sanctuary?
articles.description: Guwahati: Khamrenga Beel, a well-known wetland at Chandrapur on the outskirts of Guwahati, is being buried under earth for the Guwahati Ring Road project. People living nearby say the beel is slowly disappearing. It lies right beside the Amchang Wildlife Sanctuary. Local sources said the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) is cutting two hills close to the sanctuary, and the soil is being dumped into the beel to fill it up. The beel is a regular spot for wild elephants from the sanctuary. Herds come down every day to drink water and play in the shallows. When winter sets in, migratory birds of many species fly in and rest here. Locals fear that all this will end if the wetland is gone. Pictures from the site show that the work is going on in full swing. A JCB excavator and dumper trucks can be seen working at the spot, with soil being carried in and dumped into the wetland. The pictures make it clear that this is not a plan on paper. Earth-moving work is already underway at Khamrenga, and a large part of the beel has been covered. Farmers are worried too. Families living along the edge of the beel grow crops on the land around it and earn their living from farming. If the beel is filled, locals say, these families could face a serious loss of income. There is also a resort in the middle of the beel, a spot visitors have long enjoyed for its calm water and open views. Locals say the ring road is now seen passing right through the middle of this area, close to the resort. The sight has left many people asking how a road can cut through the heart of a wetland that is also a home for elephants and birds. Khamrenga Beel is in Thakurkuchi village of Chandrapur, about 38 km from Guwahati. It is a freshwater wetland and part of the larger Amchang landscape. It is known as an important bird area, and bird lovers say it is home to several resident and migratory species, including endangered vultures and the spot-billed pelican. The beel is also a popular picnic and bird-watching spot, and it has a small natural island in it. The best time to visit is from November to February. Every year towards the end of the year, local communities gather for the Khamrenga Beel Festival, a community fishing event held when the water level drops in winter. About the Guwahati Ring Road project The Guwahati Ring Road is a 121-km project being carried out by NHAI to reduce traffic pressure on the city and improve regional connectivity. Different reports put the cost between Rs 5,700 crore and Rs 6,000 crore. It is being built on the Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) model, and the contract has gone to Ahmedabad-based Dineshchandra R Agrawal Infracon Pvt Ltd. The concession agreement was signed in April 2025. The project has three parts: A new 56-km, four-lane, access-controlled Northern Guwahati Bypass. Widening of NH-27 from four lanes to six lanes over a stretch of about 8 km between Khanapara and Sonapur. Upgrading of an existing 58-km bypass along NH-27. The plan also includes a new bridge over the Brahmaputra. The route passes through Baihata Chariali, Kamalpur, Karara, Mandakata, Chandrapur and Sonapur. Environmental worries about the project are not new. In early 2026, NorthEast Now reported that Khamrenga Beel and Borbila Beel were likely to be directly affected by the alignment. Borbila Beel, spread over nearly 929 hectares in Chandrapur Circle, is another important freshwater wetland. According to NHAI's proposal, as reported by the Sentinel, the project needs 7.12 hectares of forest land inside Amchang Wildlife Sanctuary and 44.60 hectares of non-forest land in its eco-sensitive zone. That adds up to roughly 51.7 hectares. The Wildlife Institute of India had suggested changing the alignment so that the road runs along the boundary of the sanctuary, to protect it. Forest officials have confirmed that 2,224 trees inside the sanctuary will have to be cut. Across the whole project, around 4,500 trees are estimated to be felled, and at least 2,000 of them fall on the Khanapara-Sonapur stretch. Hills in the Amchang range are also to be cut at several places to make room for the six-lane highway. Environmentalists have warned that this could disturb the natural drainage from the eastern hills and make Guwahati's flooding worse. Senior advocate Kishor Kalita had said earlier that Amchang and the other green areas on the city's eastern and southern sides could suffer the same fate as Deepor Beel, which was badly damaged after a railway line was built through it. Amchang is also an important elephant habitat and movement corridor. Experts say that breaking up the habitat could increase human-elephant conflict. The matter reached the Gauhati High Court through a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) filed by social activist Arkasish Chaliha and senior journalist Mahesh Deka. It began after the Divisional Forest Officer of the Guwahati Wildlife Division issued an e-tender in February to select a contractor for felling trees inside the sanctuary and its eco-sensitive zone. The petitioners called the move premature. On April 8, a bench headed by Chief Justice Ashutosh Kumar restrained the authorities from finalising the tender. The state had assured the court that the tender would not be finalised until the next hearing, which was set for April 23. On May 7, the court directed NHAI and the Centre to file detailed affidavits on whether all required environmental and wildlife clearances had been taken before work began. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change was also asked to state clearly whether all preconditions for the project had been met. During that hearing, Assam's Additional Advocate General P.N. Goswami told the court that no trees would be cut for the time being. The petitioners also pointed to an annual compliance report submitted by NHAI on August 4, 2025, to the Divisional Forest Officer of the Guwahati Wildlife Division. They said important columns, including those on the comprehensive study and the project's impact on wildlife, were left blank. They argued that allowing forest diversion and tree felling without an independent study would go against the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Rules, 2023. According to Law Trend, the High Court later disposed of the PIL after the state government and NHAI gave assurances to protect wildlife habitats. The report said the Standing Committee of the National Board for Wildlife had already given conditional approval. The petitioners had made clear from the start that they were not against the ring road itself, only against the alignment passing through the sanctuary. Villagers and conservation groups now want the filling of Khamrenga Beel stopped at once. They want the authorities to say who permitted the filling of the wetland, and to confirm whether it is covered by the assurances given in court. They also want the road alignment reviewed so that the beel, the elephant movement path and the farmland around it are protected.

articles.title: Rs 10,000 crore SME Growth Fund gets Cabinet nod, manufacturing firms to get majority allocation
articles.description: The Union Cabinet has approved a Rs 10,000 crore government commitment towards setting up an SME Growth Fund (SGF), aimed at providing growth equity to SME seeking to expand their businesses. The decision was taken at a Cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Under the plan, the Government of India will commit an aggregate Rs 10,000 crore to an Alternative Investment Fund (AIF) established under the SGF framework. The fund , announced in the Union Budget 2026-27, is intended to address what the government describes as a structural gap in the availability of equity capital for SME. Existing funds provide equity support to businesses, but the government said many are focused on early-stage enterprises and predominantly cover micro enterprises. Majority allocation to manufacturing SMEs A majority of the SGF's allocation will be directed towards SME focused on manufacturing. The fund will provide what the government calls “patient growth equity capital” to high-potential SMEs that have demonstrated business viability and the ability to scale. The government said long-term risk capital is needed by companies looking to expand, adopt advanced technologies, enter international markets, undertake acquisitions and grow into larger businesses. The SGF is intended to provide capital that can help SMEs expand operations, invest in technology and manufacturing capacity, enter overseas markets, integrate into global value chains and undertake strategic investments . It will also consider SMEs operating in industrial clusters in Tier-II and Tier-III cities. The government expects investment in these clusters to support regional industrial development, strengthen local supply chains and generate employment. Fund seeks to address growth-stage financing gap The government said that while measures have improved access to credit for SMEs, a gap remains in the availability of long-term risk capital for businesses that have moved beyond their early stages and are seeking further growth. The SGF has been designed to address this gap through equity investment in businesses with demonstrated viability and scalability. Apart from manufacturing, the initiative will cover enterprises operating in services, technology, innovation-driven sectors and strategic value chains. For manufacturing businesses, the government expects the fund to support capacity expansion and technology adoption, while improving productivity and export competitiveness as companies achieve greater scale. SMEs are significant contributors to India's employment, exports, manufacturing output and innovation, making access to growth capital an important issue for companies seeking to expand beyond their existing operations. Part of wider MSME support measures The SME Growth Fund was proposed in the Union Budget 2026-27 as part of measures to provide equity, liquidity and professional support to the wider MSME ecosystem. The government said the initiative will complement measures including credit-support mechanisms, digitalisation programmes, ease-of-doing-business reforms, public procurement reforms, startup promotion initiatives and production-linked incentive schemes. It expects the fund to help develop a pipeline of Indian companies with the scale, innovation capabilities and competitiveness required to become leading businesses in their respective sectors. The initiative has also been linked to the government's Viksit Bharat 2047 vision, including efforts to deepen India's domestic capital market for growth-stage businesses and build companies capable of competing internationally. “By catalysing investment in high-growth SMEs, the Fund will help create champions, drive innovation-led industrialization, and generate quality employment opportunities,” the government said.

articles.title: Approves Rs 10,000-cr SME Growth Fund
articles.description: New Delhi, Oct 6: The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Tuesday approved the government’s commitment of Rs 10,000 crore towards the establishment of the SME Growth Fund (SGF) to provide direct equity investments to small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and help create a new generation of Indian companies capable of competing globally. The initiative is part of the measures announced in the Union Budget 2026-27 to provide equity, liquidity and professional support to the MSME ecosystem. The government said existing funds provide equity support to enterprises, but most focus on early-stage businesses and largely cover micro enterprises. A structural gap, it said, remains in the availability of growth-stage equity capital for small and medium enterprises. The SGF is aimed at catalysing growth-oriented capital for SMEs across manufacturing, services, technology, innovation-driven sectors and strategic value chains. The government said the initiative would address the financing gap faced by viable SMEs seeking to scale operations, innovate, expand internationally, adopt advanced technologies, undertake acquisitions and emerge as industry leaders. The fund will provide “patient growth equity capital” to high-potential SMEs with demonstrated business viability and scalability. A majority of the fund’s allocation will be directed towards small and medium manufacturing-focused enterprises. It will also consider SMEs operating in industrial clusters in Tier-II and Tier-III cities. By providing long-term capital, the initiative is expected to help Indian SMEs expand capacity, adopt advanced technologies, enter international markets, integrate into global value chains and undertake strategic investments. The government said the fund would help create a strong pipeline of Indian companies with the scale, innovation capabilities and competitiveness required to become champions in their respective sectors. Under the initiative, the Government of India will provide an aggregate commitment of Rs 10,000 crore to an Alternative Investment Fund (AIF) established under the SGF framework. The government said the fund would complement existing measures to strengthen the SME sector, including digitalisation initiatives, credit support mechanisms, ease of doing business reforms, public procurement reforms, startup promotion initiatives and production-linked incentive programmes. The SGF is also expected to support balanced regional industrial development by investing in industrial clusters, including those in Tier-II and Tier-III cities. Such investments, the government said, would strengthen local supply chains and generate quality employment opportunities. The initiative is part of the government’s broader effort to strengthen India’s entrepreneurship ecosystem, deepen the domestic capital market for growth-stage enterprises and advance the vision of Viksit Bharat @2047.
